solution: The complement \(A'\) consists of the elements of \(U\) that are not in \(A\). Removing \(1, 2, 3, 4\) from \(U = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9\}\) leaves \(A' = \{5, 6, 7, 8, 9\}\).
Delete the elements of \(B = \{2, 4, 6, 8\}\) from \(U = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9\}\). The elements left are the odd ones, so \(B' = \{1, 3, 5, 7, 9\}\).
First take the union: \(A \cup C = \{1, 2, 3, 4\} \cup \{3, 4, 5, 6\} = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\). Removing these from \(U\) gives \((A \cup C)' = \{7, 8, 9\}\).
First take the union: \(A \cup B = \{1, 2, 3, 4\} \cup \{2, 4, 6, 8\} = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8\}\). Removing these from \(U\) gives \((A \cup B)' = \{5, 7, 9\}\).
From part (i), \(A' = \{5, 6, 7, 8, 9\}\). Taking the complement again removes these from \(U\), leaving \((A')' = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\), which is \(A\) itself. This illustrates the law \((A')' = A\).

The difference \(B - C\) keeps the elements of \(B\) that are not in \(C\). Here \(4\) and \(6\) lie in \(C = \{3, 4, 5, 6\}\) while \(2\) and \(8\) do not, so \(B - C = \{2, 8\}\). Removing these from \(U\) gives \((B - C)' = \{1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9\}\).
Remove the letters of \(A = \{a, b, c\}\) from \(U = \{a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h\}\). Hence \(A' = \{d, e, f, g, h\}\).
Remove the letters of \(B = \{d, e, f, g\}\) from \(U = \{a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h\}\). Hence \(B' = \{a, b, c, h\}\).
Remove the letters of \(C = \{a, c, e, g\}\) from \(U = \{a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h\}\). Hence \(C' = \{b, d, f, h\}\).
Remove the letters of \(D = \{f, g, h, a\}\) from \(U = \{a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h\}\). Hence \(D' = \{b, c, d, e\}\).

Here the universal set is \(\mathbf{N}\). Every natural number is either even or odd, so deleting the even natural numbers from \(\mathbf{N}\) leaves exactly the odd ones. Hence the complement is \(\{x : x \in \mathbf{N} \text{ and } x \text{ is an odd natural number}\}\).
With \(\mathbf{N}\) as the universal set, a natural number that is not odd is even. Hence the complement is \(\{x : x \in \mathbf{N} \text{ and } x \text{ is an even natural number}\}\).

The given set is \(\{3, 6, 9, 12, \ldots\}\), the multiples of \(3\) in \(\mathbf{N}\). Its complement keeps every natural number that \(3\) does not divide, so the complement is \(\{x : x \in \mathbf{N} \text{ and } x \text{ is not a multiple of } 3\}\).

Deleting the primes from \(\mathbf{N}\) leaves \(1\) together with all the composite numbers. Hence the complement is \(\{x : x \in \mathbf{N} \text{ and } x \text{ is not a prime number}\}\), that is \(\{1, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, \ldots\}\).

A natural number divisible by both \(3\) and \(5\) is divisible by their l.c.m. \(15\), so the given set is \(\{15, 30, 45, \ldots\}\). Its complement therefore keeps every natural number that is not a multiple of \(15\), so the complement is \(\{x : x \in \mathbf{N} \text{ and } x \text{ is not divisible by } 3 \text{ and } 5\}\), i.e. \(\{x : x \in \mathbf{N}, x \text{ is not a multiple of } 15\}\).

The given set is \(\{1, 4, 9, 16, \ldots\}\). Deleting it from \(\mathbf{N}\) leaves every natural number that is not the square of a natural number, so the complement is \(\{x : x \in \mathbf{N} \text{ and } x \text{ is not a perfect square}\}\).

The given set is \(\{1, 8, 27, 64, \ldots\}\). Deleting it from \(\mathbf{N}\) leaves every natural number that is not the cube of a natural number, so the complement is \(\{x : x \in \mathbf{N} \text{ and } x \text{ is not a perfect cube}\}\).

Solving \(x + 5 = 8\) gives \(x = 3\), so the given set is \(\{3\}\). Its complement in \(\mathbf{N}\) is every natural number other than \(3\), that is \(\{x : x \in \mathbf{N} \text{ and } x \ne 3\}\).

Solving \(2x + 5 = 9\) gives \(2x = 4\), so \(x = 2\) and the given set is \(\{2\}\). Its complement in \(\mathbf{N}\) is every natural number other than \(2\), that is \(\{x : x \in \mathbf{N} \text{ and } x \ne 2\}\).
The given set is \(\{7, 8, 9, 10, \ldots\}\). The natural numbers left out are those with \(x < 7\), so the complement is \(\{x : x \in \mathbf{N} \text{ and } x < 7\} = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\).

From \(2x + 1 > 10\) we get \(2x > 9\), so \(x > \frac{9}{2}\). The natural numbers satisfying this are \(5, 6, 7, \ldots\), so the given set is \(\{5, 6, 7, \ldots\}\). Its complement is \(\{x : x \in \mathbf{N} \text{ and } 2x + 1 \le 10\} = \{x : x \in \mathbf{N} \text{ and } x \le \frac{9}{2}\} = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\).

Compute each side separately for \(U = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9\}\), \(A = \{2, 4, 6, 8\}\), \(B = \{2, 3, 5, 7\}\). Left side: \(A \cup B = \{2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8\}\), and the elements of \(U\) left out are \(1\) and \(9\), so \((A \cup B)' = \{1, 9\}\). Right side: \(A' = \{1, 3, 5, 7, 9\}\) and \(B' = \{1, 4, 6, 8, 9\}\); the elements common to both are \(1\) and \(9\), so \(A' \cap B' = \{1, 9\}\). Both sides equal \(\{1, 9\}\), hence \((A \cup B)' = A' \cap B'\) is verified.

Compute each side separately. Left side: the only element common to \(A = \{2, 4, 6, 8\}\) and \(B = \{2, 3, 5, 7\}\) is \(2\), so \(A \cap B = \{2\}\) and \((A \cap B)' = \{1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9\}\). Right side: \(A' = \{1, 3, 5, 7, 9\}\) and \(B' = \{1, 4, 6, 8, 9\}\), so \(A' \cup B' = \{1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9\}\). Both sides list the same eight elements, hence \((A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'\) is verified.

Draw a rectangle for the universal set \(U\) and inside it two overlapping circles labelled \(A\) and \(B\). The set \(A \cup B\) is the whole of the two circles taken together, so its complement is everything else. Shade the part of the rectangle that lies outside both circles; no part of either circle is shaded.

Draw the rectangle \(U\) with two overlapping circles \(A\) and \(B\). Here \(A'\) is the whole region outside circle \(A\) and \(B'\) is the whole region outside circle \(B\); a point belongs to \(A' \cap B'\) only if it lies outside \(A\) and also outside \(B\). So shade the part of the rectangle lying outside both circles. This is the same shaded region as for \((A \cup B)'\), which illustrates De Morgan's law \((A \cup B)' = A' \cap B'\).

Draw the rectangle \(U\) with two overlapping circles \(A\) and \(B\). The set \(A \cap B\) is only the lens-shaped region where the two circles overlap, so its complement is everything except that lens. Shade the whole rectangle except the overlap, that is: the part of \(A\) outside \(B\), the part of \(B\) outside \(A\), and the region outside both circles; leave the overlap unshaded.

Draw the rectangle \(U\) with two overlapping circles \(A\) and \(B\). A point belongs to \(A' \cup B'\) if it lies outside \(A\) or outside \(B\), which fails only for a point lying inside both circles. So shade the whole rectangle except the lens-shaped overlap. This is the same shaded region as for \((A \cap B)'\), which illustrates De Morgan's law \((A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'\).

A triangle lies in \(A'\) exactly when it fails the condition defining \(A\), that is when it does not have at least one angle different from \(60^\circ\). So every angle of such a triangle must equal \(60^\circ\), which makes it equiangular and hence equilateral. Therefore \(A' = \{x : x \text{ is an equilateral triangle in the plane}\}\).
Every element of \(U\) either lies in \(A\) or fails to lie in \(A\), and in the second case it lies in \(A'\). So the union covers the whole universal set, giving \(A \cup A' = U\).

The empty set contains no element of \(U\), so every element of \(U\) lies in its complement, giving \(\phi' = U\). Hence \(\phi' \cap A = U \cap A = A\), since \(A \subset U\). So the blank is \(A\).
An element of \(A \cap A'\) would have to lie in \(A\) and simultaneously not lie in \(A\), which is impossible. So no such element exists and \(A \cap A' = \phi\).
No element of \(U\) lies outside \(U\), so \(U' = \phi\). Hence \(U' \cap A = \phi \cap A = \phi\), since the empty set has no element to share with \(A\). So the blank is \(\phi\).

First find \(A\) in roster form. Factorising, \(x^{2} - 8x + 12 = (x - 2)(x - 6) = 0\), so \(x = 2\) or \(x = 6\) and \(A = \{2, 6\}\). Also \(B = \{2, 4, 6\}\), \(C = \{2, 4, 6, 8, \ldots\}\) is the set of even natural numbers and \(D = \{6\}\). Now compare: \(6 \in A\), so \(D \subset A\); both \(2\) and \(6\) lie in \(B\), so \(A \subset B\); every element of \(B\) is an even natural number, so \(B \subset C\). Chaining these, \(D \subset A \subset B \subset C\). Hence the inclusions among the four sets are \(D \subset A\), \(D \subset B\), \(D \subset C\), \(A \subset B\), \(A \subset C\) and \(B \subset C\).

The statement is false, because \(A \in B\) says that \(A\) is an element of \(B\), not that its members are. For a counter-example take \(A = \{1\}\) and \(B = \{\{1\}, 2\}\), and let \(x = 1\). Then \(x \in A\) and \(A \in B\), but the elements of \(B\) are \(\{1\}\) and \(2\), so \(x = 1 \notin B\). Hence the statement is false.

The statement is false. Take \(A = \{1\}\), \(B = \{1, 2\}\) and \(C = \{\{1, 2\}, 3\}\). Then \(A \subset B\) and \(B \in C\), but the elements of \(C\) are \(\{1, 2\}\) and \(3\), and \(A = \{1\}\) is neither of them, so \(A \notin C\). Hence the statement is false.

The statement is true. Let \(x\) be any element of \(A\). Since \(A \subset B\), we get \(x \in B\); and since \(B \subset C\), this gives \(x \in C\). Thus every element of \(A\) is an element of \(C\), so \(A \subset C\). Hence the statement is true.

The statement is true; it is the contrapositive of the definition of a subset. Suppose, on the contrary, that \(x \in A\). Since \(A \subset B\), this forces \(x \in B\), which contradicts the hypothesis \(x \notin B\). Hence \(x\) cannot belong to \(A\), that is \(x \notin A\). So the statement is true.

Start from \(B\) and use the absorption law \(B \cap (A \cup B) = B\): \(B = B \cap (A \cup B) = B \cap (A \cup C)\), using the hypothesis \(A \cup B = A \cup C\). By the distributive law, \(B \cap (A \cup C) = (B \cap A) \cup (B \cap C)\). Since \(A \cap B = A \cap C\), this equals \((A \cap C) \cup (B \cap C)\), which by the distributive law again is \((A \cup B) \cap C\). Using the hypothesis once more, \((A \cup B) \cap C = (A \cup C) \cap C = C\) by absorption. Combining the chain, \(B = C\).

The four conditions are proved equivalent by closing the cycle (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii) \(\Rightarrow\) (iii) \(\Rightarrow\) (iv) \(\Rightarrow\) (i). Here we establish the first link, that \(A \subset B\) implies \(A - B = \phi\). Suppose some \(x \in A - B\). Then \(x \in A\) and \(x \notin B\); but \(A \subset B\) forces \(x \in B\), a contradiction. So no such \(x\) exists, and \(A - B = \phi\).

Continuing the cycle, we show that \(A - B = \phi\) implies \(A \cup B = B\). If \(A - B = \phi\), then no element of \(A\) lies outside \(B\), so every \(x \in A\) satisfies \(x \in B\), i.e. \(A \subset B\). Hence every element of \(A \cup B\) lies in \(B\), giving \(A \cup B \subset B\); and \(B \subset A \cup B\) always holds. Therefore \(A \cup B = B\).

Continuing the cycle, we show that \(A \cup B = B\) implies \(A \cap B = A\). Since \(A \subset A \cup B = B\), we have \(A \subset B\). Then every element of \(A\) lies in \(B\) as well, so \(A \subset A \cap B\); and \(A \cap B \subset A\) always holds. Therefore \(A \cap B = A\).

This closes the cycle: we show that \(A \cap B = A\) implies \(A \subset B\). Let \(x \in A\). Then \(x \in A \cap B\), because \(A \cap B = A\), and every element of \(A \cap B\) lies in \(B\); hence \(x \in B\). So \(A \subset B\). With the three earlier links this completes the chain \(A \subset B \Rightarrow A - B = \phi \Rightarrow A \cup B = B \Rightarrow A \cap B = A \Rightarrow A \subset B\), so all four conditions are equivalent.

Use \(A - B = A \cap B'\) and the distributive law. For the first result, \((A \cap B) \cup (A - B) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap B') = A \cap (B \cup B') = A \cap U = A\). For the second, \(A \cup (B - A) = A \cup (B \cap A') = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup A') = (A \cup B) \cap U = A \cup B\). Hence \(A = (A \cap B) \cup (A - B)\) and \(A \cup (B - A) = A \cup B\).

Write the first \(A\) as \(A \cap U\) and apply the distributive law: \(A \cup (A \cap B) = (A \cap U) \cup (A \cap B) = A \cap (U \cup B) = A \cap U = A\), since \(U \cup B = U\) for every \(B \subset U\). Hence \(A \cup (A \cap B) = A\).

Write the first \(A\) as \(A \cup \phi\) and apply the distributive law: \(A \cap (A \cup B) = (A \cup \phi) \cap (A \cup B) = A \cup (\phi \cap B) = A \cup \phi = A\), since \(\phi \cap B = \phi\) for every \(B\). Hence \(A \cap (A \cup B) = A\).

It is enough to exhibit one example in which the equality of the intersections holds while the two sets differ. Take \(A = \{1, 2\}\), \(B = \{2, 3\}\) and \(C = \{2, 4\}\). The only element common to \(A\) and \(B\) is \(2\), so \(A \cap B = \{2\}\); likewise the only element common to \(A\) and \(C\) is \(2\), so \(A \cap C = \{2\}\). Thus \(A \cap B = A \cap C\), yet \(3 \in B\) while \(3 \notin C\), so \(B \ne C\). Hence \(A \cap B = A \cap C\) need not imply \(B = C\).

Use the hint. By absorption, \(A = A \cap (A \cup X)\), and since \(A \cup X = B \cup X\) this equals \(A \cap (B \cup X)\). By the distributive law, \(A \cap (B \cup X) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap X) = (A \cap B) \cup \phi = A \cap B\), using \(A \cap X = \phi\). Similarly \(B = B \cap (B \cup X) = B \cap (A \cup X) = (B \cap A) \cup (B \cap X) = (A \cap B) \cup \phi = A \cap B\), using \(B \cap X = \phi\). Both \(A\) and \(B\) therefore equal \(A \cap B\), so \(A = B\).

Choose three sets in which each pair shares an element, but no element is shared by all three. Take \(A = \{1, 2\}\), \(B = \{2, 3\}\) and \(C = \{1, 3\}\). Then \(A \cap B = \{2\}\), \(B \cap C = \{3\}\) and \(A \cap C = \{1\}\), so all three pairwise intersections are non-empty. But \(A \cap B \cap C = \{2\} \cap \{1, 3\} = \phi\), since the common element of each pair is missing from the third set. Hence \(A = \{1, 2\}\), \(B = \{2, 3\}\), \(C = \{1, 3\}\) is a required example.
